entries.html:
Spent yesterday at the Englewood Chamber of Commerce for an SBDC event on AI. Walked in without expectations and left with a sharp reminder: meat space and internet space are completely different worlds.

On the internet — looking at what other builders are shipping, the tooling they're using, the projects on 014 and beyond — it's easy to feel behind. The pace feels fast, the competition feels dense, and everyone seems to be further along.

In a room of actual business owners and operators? The dynamic flips entirely. It became clear that I was the most experienced person in the room when it came to AI. Not because the bar was low — but because these people are simply not on X or in the builder communities where this stuff is discussed. The hunger to use these tools is real and it's enormous. The distribution gap between "builder Twitter" and Main Street business owners is bigger than I'd appreciated.

The other thing: showing up counts. Just by attending a single event, I connected with four businesses that want to talk. No funnel, no cold email, no ad spend. Just presence.

Lesson candidate: offline rooms are a distribution unlock that internet-native builders systematically underestimate.

entries.html:
A lot of thinking lately about how AI-assisted building changes the way reps can succeed or fail — and it comes down to methodology.

When you don't spend enough time defining your architecture, product, and interface decisions before you start vibe coding, you bake in technical debt fast. The earlier reps suffered from this. The lesson: spend substantially more time on back-end structure and organization, define the product and front-end interface choices, and then write code.

The other thing I'm learning: build harder MVPs that let you vet ideas faster.

Rep 006 — Teshuvah Read Along: Spent a lot of time building it out, and now I'm going to have to gut it and rebuild from the ground up. We met with a collaborating rabbi who has a beautiful siddur that's quite different from what's baked into the current app — which means a full rebuild. That said, not much is truly lost. The core functionality — the read-along mechanic and continuous scroll — has been refined through the process. The foundation is solid even if the structure has to change.

Rep 013 — Civic Transparency Tool: Took the opposite approach. Launched the dumbest possible version — not a responsive aggregation platform, just a tool that reviews existing videos and generates a newsletter. People love it. The response has been almost immediate. It took substantially less time to build. This is the template for how MVPs should work.

Rep 021 — n-of-one: Built as a stripped-down version of the original stack tracker concept, not architected as a standalone app — it runs on my existing setup and is built just for me. One user. But I'm the user, and I'm learning fast. If I ever want to turn it into a broader platform, the architecture will need to change significantly for other users. But for now it validates the problem immediately, which is the whole point.

The through-line: a dumb, fast thing that proves the idea beats a well-built thing that proves nothing.

entries.html:
013 Eyes on Arvada launched today — posted to Reddit, published the newsletter, reached out to city council members directly. For the first time across all the reps, there was immediate, genuine signal that people cared. Not just pageviews or politeness — actual interest.

What's notable is that the why isn't fully clear yet. It works, but there's no clean explanation for why this one landed when others didn't. That ambiguity is worth sitting with rather than rushing to explain away. The instinct is to reverse-engineer a formula, but the more honest read is: follow the signal first, understand it later.

The rep is also different in character from everything else. Most reps are about reach and scale — get it in front of as many people as possible. This one is the opposite. It's hyper-local, deliberately small, and requires actual human engagement with stakeholders in a new domain. That friction turned out to be a feature. Getting out and talking to people in a specific community produced a response that broadcasting to a general audience never did.

There's something potentially fat-tailed about the hyperlocal + AI angle that hasn't been fully explored. The same pipeline could work for any municipality. But scaling it thoughtfully — maybe city by city, each with a local operator — is a very different model than most of the reps. That's worth a dedicated strategy session before assuming it should scale the same way everything else does.

Monetization is genuinely unclear right now, and that's okay. The instinct to solve it immediately is a trap — the right move is to grow the audience first and let the monetization model emerge from what the audience actually values. Advertising, sponsorships, a paid tier for civic organizations, a licensing model for other cities — all of these are on the table but none should be forced yet.

A meeting with the Arvada mayor is scheduled for next week. That's a new kind of stakeholder relationship — one that doesn't fit the usual founder-to-customer pattern. Worth being thoughtful about how to show up in that conversation.

016 Stock Up Dinners is close to launch. In the middle of that push, a realization surfaced: the other businesses have been getting almost no attention. The root cause isn't distraction — it's that most of those ideas aren't fleshed out enough yet to have clear next steps. Without a clear next step, it's too easy to skip.

Plan for today: carve out time to go through every active rep and re-vet each idea before assigning next steps. No moving forward on anything that hasn't been re-assessed.

The other thread worth addressing: 002 Estate Sale Helper and 016 Stock Up Dinners are both live or nearly live, and neither has a real distribution strategy yet. The immediate priority is demand validation before committing to paid ads — need some signal that people want this before putting money behind it. Organic first.

Once paid ads do start, AI tooling looks like a real leverage point there — from creative generation to targeting logic to iteration speed. Worth thinking about structuring that as a repeatable playbook rather than doing it ad hoc each time.

entries.html:
Build to Throw Away

As easy as it is to build, it's just as easy to throw away.

Spent a good chunk of this morning remapping Stock Up Dinners against the new understanding of what the product actually needs to be — and landed on the conclusion that the existing build has to be gutted. Not patched. Not extended. Rebuilt from a new foundation.

This isn't a failure. It's the natural consequence of building before designing. The work moved fast; the direction was wrong. When the foundation is wrong, there's no reasonable expectation the thing on top of it will succeed. Better to recognize it early and reset than to keep building on a cracked slab.

The lesson: be ready to throw it away. Not recklessly — but without attachment. The hard work is appropriate design and putting the elements in the right places. Speed of execution only matters if the execution is pointed at something real.

AI Architecture Is the Missing Piece

Had a conversation with Rabbi Leban today through Colorado AI Lab. What stood out: people can intuit that AI has clear benefits for their organization — they feel it. What they're missing is the architecture.

The questions that come up are real and disorienting: Do I throw everything away? Do I rebuild? Do I add new tools on top of what I have? Do I just improve what's already there?

Organizations need a way to think about this, not just a list of tools. The worst thing you can do is throw a bunch of AI solutions at someone who doesn't yet understand the problem they're solving for. The tools are the easy part. The architecture — understanding which problems to solve, in what order, with what approach — is where the actual value is created.

That's the work Colorado AI Lab is positioned to do.

Working on 016 today and hit a clarifying moment that's worth recording.

AI Speeds You Up Into the Wrong Place

AI is a powerful accelerator — but it accelerates you toward building, not toward thinking. The risk is that you move fast into the wrong direction before you've done the hard work of understanding the process your users actually go through.

That's what happened here. The early hours went into designing an app — menus, meal types, one-off cooking vs. weekly prep. It felt like progress. It looked like progress. But it was building the end product before understanding the entry point.

The Real Unlock: Pantry Tracking

The core insight today: the most valuable thing Stock Up Dinners can do is not tell people what to cook — it's tracking what they already have.

Once the pantry is tracked: - Shopping lists write themselves (buy what you're actually missing) - Recipe recommendations become immediately relevant (use what's already there) - The product gets smarter the more someone uses it

Everything else — the 14 meal plans, the Costco shopping list lead magnet, the recipe browsing — these are acquisition surfaces. The pantry tracker is the retention engine and the value core.

Process Before Product

The lead magnet work (Costco staples list + 14 meals) turned out to be generative, not just promotional. Building it forced the question: after someone downloads this and cooks a few meals, what does the ongoing relationship with this product look like?

That question led directly to pantry tracking as the answer.

The lesson isn't to skip product thinking — it's to start with the user's ongoing process, not the final feature set. The app design got complicated because it started in the wrong place. Now there's a clear foundation to rebuild from.

entries.html:
Milestone: 20 reps. And with it, the first real sense of rep fatigue — not from volume, but from a pattern emerging in how reps stall.

The Holding-Pattern Problem

Reps seem to hit a plateau state where progress requires one of two things:

  1. Product execution — building new features, improving the core experience. 002 is the example here: it's live, but the next level requires shipping more functionality. That work falls on the human.

  2. Active selling — going out and closing. 014 is the example: the funnel exists, the assets are ready, but someone has to actually send the messages and get on calls. That also falls on the human.

Both bottlenecks currently require human execution, and at 20 reps, those accumulate faster than they clear.

018 is the outlier — it's in a stable holding state that doesn't demand either. It just exists and works. That's a different kind of rep.

The Question

Is there a useful new categorization for reps in this plateau state? Something beyond live that signals what kind of human action is blocking the next level — execution vs. selling? And is there an AI leverage point that could absorb one or both of those gaps over time?

No answers yet. Just noticing the shape of the problem at 20 reps.

First field note. The pattern across 011 and 014 is the same: I keep building the product and not the distribution. Cold outreach by hand is the only thing that's ever moved a needle.

This realization is the seed of distribution-beats-craft.
